```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# HTML figures are drawn as PNG and kept as WebP: lossless, or lossy at quality 90 when that is less than half the
# size. The PDF figures stay vector graphics. Any failure of magick (not installed, no WebP, or a broken
# installation whose system libraries are missing) keeps the PNG
webp <- function(path) {
  if (knitr::is_latex_output() || !grepl(pattern = "[.]png$", x = path)) return(path)
  tryCatch(
      {
        if (!requireNamespace("magick", quietly = TRUE) || !isTRUE(magick::magick_config()$webp)) return(path)
        img <- magick::image_read(path)
        out <- sub(pattern = "[.]png$", replacement = ".webp", x = path)
        tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".webp")
        magick::image_write(
            image   = img
          , path    = out
          , format  = "webp"
          , quality = 100
          , defines = c(`webp:lossless` = "true")
          )
        magick::image_write(image = img, path = tmp, format = "webp", quality = 90)
        if (file.size(tmp) < file.size(out) / 2) file.copy(from = tmp, to = out, overwrite = TRUE)
        unlink(c(path, tmp))
        out
      }
    , error = function(e) path
    )
}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = FALSE, comment = "", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2,
                      dev = if (knitr::is_latex_output()) "cairo_pdf" else "ragg_png", dpi = 96,
                      fig.process = webp)
if (requireNamespace("mhpfilter", quietly = TRUE)) library(mhpfilter) else
  pkgload::load_all(export_all = FALSE, helpers = FALSE, quiet = TRUE)
```

# Abstract

**mhpfilter** splits a macroeconomic time series into a trend and a cycle. This vignette takes the quarterly real GDP
of the United States from the raw series to the three filters of the package, their comparison, many series at once
and a plain-language reading of the results. The later vignettes give the theory (vignette 2), the two papers behind
the package (vignettes 3 and 4), the simulation study (vignette 5), the application (vignette 6) and the checks of
the code (vignette 7).

# The data

`us_macro` holds quarterly real GDP, consumption and investment of the United States from 1959 to 2009 (FRED). As a
`ts` the series keeps its dates, and every result of the package keeps them too.

```{r data}
data(us_macro)
head(us_macro)
gdp <- ts(data = us_macro$gdp, start = c(1959, 1), frequency = 4)
```

# Three filters

## The HP filter

The filter of Hodrick and Prescott (1997) fits a smooth trend $\vg$ to the series $\vx$ by minimising
$$
\sum_{t=1}^{T}(x_t - g_t)^2 + \lambda\sum_{t=2}^{T-1}\left[(g_{t+1} - g_t) - (g_t - g_{t-1})\right]^2 ,
$$
and the cycle is $\vc = \vx - \vg$. The smoothing parameter $\lambda$ is conventionally 1600 for quarterly data. On
the logarithm of a series the cycle is close to the percentage deviation from the trend.

```{r hp}
hp <-
  hp_filter(
      x         = log(gdp)
    , lambda    = 1600
    , as_dt     = TRUE
    , log_scale = FALSE
    )
hp
```

With `as_dt = TRUE`, the default kept from version 0.1.0, the result is a `data.table`; `as_dt = FALSE` gives a list
with methods for printing and plotting.

## The modified HP filter

The modified HP filter of McDermott (1997), assessed by Choudhary, Hanif and Iqbal (2014), lets the data choose
$\lambda$: it tries every $\lambda = 1, 2, \dots$ and keeps the one that minimises a generalised cross-validation
criterion.

```{r mhp}
mhp <-
  mhp_filter(
      x          = log(gdp)
    , max_lambda = 100000
    , as_dt      = FALSE
    , log_scale  = FALSE
    , criterion  = "approximate"
    )
mhp
```

```{r mhp-plot, fig.height = 5}
plot(x = mhp)
```

```{r mhp-gcv}
plot(x = mhp, which = "gcv")
```

## The fully modified HP filter

The HP filter has too little information at the ends of a series, so its trend follows the last observations too
closely and the end of the cycle is biased towards zero, just where a policy maker needs it most. The fully
modified HP filter of Hanif, Iqbal and Choudhary (2017) raises $\lambda$ at the first and last observations, with
weights chosen to make the filter at the ends behave like the filter in the middle, and chooses $\lambda$ from the
data as the modified HP filter does. The published code filters the logarithm of the series and returns the trend
and the cycle in levels; `log_scale = TRUE` does the same.

```{r fmhp}
fm <-
  fmhp_filter(
      x               = gdp
    , max_lambda      = 3000
    , k_linear        = 15
    , k_quadratic     = NULL
    , alpha_linear    = seq(from = 0, to = 2000, by = 10)
    , alpha_quadratic = seq(from = 0, to = 2000, by = 5)
    , schemes         = c("linear", "quadratic")
    , form            = "rows"
    , lambda          = NULL
    , log_scale       = TRUE
    , as_dt           = FALSE
    )
fm
fm$schemes
```

```{r fmhp-lambda}
plot(x = fm, which = "lambda")
```

The smoothing parameter rises from `r fm$lambda` in the middle to `r max(fm$lambda_t)` at the first and last
observation (`r fm$scheme` weights on `r fm$k` values at each end).

# Comparing the filters

`fmhp_compare()` filters the series with the three filters and compares the cycles and their end-point loss, the
measure of end-point bias used by Hanif et al. (2017): zero for a filter that treats the ends like the middle.

```{r compare}
cmp <-
  fmhp_compare(
      x          = gdp
    , frequency  = "quarterly"
    , max_lambda = 3000
    , log_scale  = TRUE
    , end_share  = 0.1
    )
cmp
```

The fully modified HP filter cuts the loss of the HP filter by more than half. Its cycle is also more variable at
the ends than in the middle, unlike the cycles of the other two filters: the end-point bias of the HP filter shows as
cycles that are too small at the ends.

```{r compare-plot, fig.height = 5.5}
plot_comparison(
    x          = log(gdp)
  , frequency  = "quarterly"
  , max_lambda = 100000
  , show_cycle = TRUE
  , fmhp       = TRUE
  )
```

# Many series

`mhp_batch()` and `fmhp_batch()` filter every column of a matrix; series of different lengths can share it, padded
with missing values at the start or the end.

```{r batch}
X <- as.matrix(us_macro[, c("gdp", "consumption", "investment")])
fb <-
  fmhp_batch(
      X               = X
    , max_lambda      = 3000
    , k_linear        = 15
    , k_quadratic     = NULL
    , alpha_linear    = seq(from = 0, to = 2000, by = 10)
    , alpha_quadratic = seq(from = 0, to = 2000, by = 5)
    , schemes         = c("linear", "quadratic")
    , form            = "rows"
    , lambda          = NULL
    , log_scale       = TRUE
    )
attr(x = fb, which = "lambdas")
```

```{r batch-plot, fig.height = 4.5}
plot_batch(
    x         = fb
  , show      = "cycle"
  , facet     = TRUE
  , highlight = NULL
  )
```

# Reading the results

`mhp_interpret()` reads a result in plain language, from its numbers, and ends with the sources of the method.

```{r interpret}
mhp_interpret(
    x   = fm
  , top = 3
  )
```

# References

Choudhary, M. A., Hanif, M. N. and Iqbal, J. (2014). On smoothing macroeconomic time series using the modified HP
filter. *Applied Economics*, 46(19), 2205--2214.

Hanif, M. N., Iqbal, J. and Choudhary, M. A. (2017). Fully modified HP filter. *SBP Working Paper Series*, No. 88,
State Bank of Pakistan.

Hodrick, R. J. and Prescott, E. C. (1997). Postwar U.S. business cycles: an empirical investigation. *Journal of
Money, Credit and Banking*, 29(1), 1--16.

McDermott, C. J. (1997). An automatic method for choosing the smoothing parameter in the HP filter. Unpublished,
International Monetary Fund.
